goal:
Make `slugify` in `src/slugify.js` turn Latin letters with diacritics into plain ASCII: `slugify("Crème Brûlée")` returns `"creme-brulee"` and `slugify("Łódź")` returns `"lodz"`.

This covers every Latin letter, not only those Unicode can split into a base letter and an accent: letters with a stroke and ligatures take their usual ASCII spelling (for example `ø` → `o`, `æ` → `ae`, `ß` → `ss`). Accents count whether the title writes them precomposed or as separate combining marks after the letter.

Keep everything that works today. In particular, letters of other scripts stay exactly as they are: `slugify` keeps Cyrillic, Greek, Japanese, and every other script unchanged, apart from lower case.

constraints: Change as few files as possible.
Delete or simplify existing code before you add code.
Write a failing test that reproduces the problem before you change any source file.

candidates.approach: Add Latin-scoped Unicode normalization inside slugify before its existing separator replacement. Process Latin letters together with their following combining marks, decompose accented letters, and remove marks only from those Latin sequences. Use a comprehensive exception map for letters normalization cannot turn into ASCII, including ł, ø, æ, and ß. Leave non-Latin sequences untouched by transliteration and retain the existing lowercase, separator, and trimming behavior.
candidates.firstStep: Add regression tests covering the requested examples, decomposed Latin accents, strokes and ligatures, non-Latin scripts, and existing separator behavior; then inventory the Latin letters requiring explicit mappings.

candidates.approach: Generate a complete Latin-to-ASCII lookup table and use it directly at runtime, without calling Unicode normalization. Build the table from a pinned Unicode Latin-letter inventory, decomposition data, and curated conventional spellings for non-decomposing letters. A scanner maps each Latin letter to its ASCII spelling and consumes combining accents attached to Latin letters, while passing other scripts through to the existing slug cleanup. This trades a larger checked-in artifact for simple, auditable runtime behavior.
candidates.firstStep: Create a generator that enumerates Unicode Latin letters and produces a coverage report showing which letters have ASCII mappings and which still require reviewed spellings.

candidates.approach: Use an established transliteration dependency rather than maintain the Latin mappings locally. Place a narrowly scoped adapter in front of the current slug cleanup: pass only Latin letter-and-mark sequences to the dependency and preserve all other sequences verbatim. Evaluate the dependency against the full Latin inventory, supplement any missing conventional spellings, and pin its version so transliteration changes do not silently alter slugs.
candidates.firstStep: Inspect the project's dependency and runtime constraints, then evaluate a candidate transliteration package against ł, ø, æ, ß, decomposed accents, and mixed-script titles before integrating it.

candidates.approach: Implement a dedicated rule-based Latin transliterator using pinned Unicode and CLDR data, rather than normalization plus exceptions or a direct character lookup. Compile Latin-to-ASCII rewrite rules into a sequence matcher that handles decomposition, combining marks, and multi-letter expansions. Keep the matcher restricted to Latin sequences and call it from slugify before the existing cleanup. This is a heavier approach, but offers a separate, reusable mechanism with explicit rule ordering and coverage validation.
candidates.firstStep: Prototype a rule compiler using the relevant Unicode decomposition and CLDR Latin-to-ASCII rules, and verify that its generated matcher changes Latin sequences without rewriting neighboring non-Latin text.
